🍞 Did the Sages Enact a Protective Ordinance for Consecrated Items?
🐐 The Yom Kippur Scapegoat Mishna — testing Rabbi Abba's framing
🔄 Two Refutations, One Answer: 'The Tanna Teaches Only the Absolute Case'
💰 Money Set Aside 'As a Guarantee' — Rabbi Ami's teaching and Rabbi Shimon's view

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Untangling the Rebbi/Rabbis Dispute From Every Angle
overview.subtitle: Temurah 23a–23b
overview.hebrewSource: מִילְּתָא דִּפְסִיקָא לֵיהּ קָתָנֵי, מִילְּתָא דְּלָא פְּסִיקָא לֵיהּ לָא קָתָנֵי
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf offers two competing accounts of what Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the Rabbis actually disagree about: Rav Huna frames it around whether the owner consulted the court before sacrificing one of two available animals, while Rabbi Abba frames it around whether atonement was achieved specifically with the LOST animal. Each framing is tested against outside sources — a baraita about preventing leftover meal offerings from becoming notar, and the Yom Kippur mishna about a rejected scapegoat's paired sin offering — and each survives only by being pinned to one side of the dispute. The mishna itself seems to refute both framings until the Gemara explains that it simply teaches the clear-cut case and leaves the disputed nuances for elsewhere. The daf closes with Rabbi Ami's ruling about money set aside merely 'as a guarantee' rather than to replace something lost, which turns out to matter specifically for Rabbi Shimon's more stringent position.

slides.title: ⚖️ Two Different Accounts of the Same Dispute
slides.subtitle: Rav Huna and Rabbi Abba each locate the Rebbi/Rabbis disagreement differently

lines.speaker: Rav Huna (citing Rav)
lines.text: Everyone agrees: if the owner just TOOK one animal and sacrificed it (without consulting the court), the other dies. They disagree only when the owner ASKS the court which to sacrifice — Rebbi: sacrifice the non-lost one (no special ordinance for consecrated items); Rabbis: sacrifice the LOST one (there IS such an ordinance).

lines.speaker: Rabbi Abba (citing Rav)
lines.text: Everyone agrees: if atonement is achieved via the NON-lost animal, the lost one dies. They disagree only when atonement is achieved via the LOST one — Rebbi: the replacement then dies too (it's 'as if' it were the lost one); Rabbis: the replacement merely grazes.

callout.label: Same conclusion, different maps:
callout.text: Both framings try to explain the mishna's two differently-worded clauses as reflecting the same underlying Rebbi/Rabbis dispute — just locating the disagreement in a different variable.

slides.title: 🍞 Testing Rav Huna: Does a Protective Ordinance Exist?
slides.subtitle: Rav Mesharshiya challenges the claim that 'no ordinance' is even a real position
rows: The Torah itself builds in mechanisms (eating with non-sacred food, or without it) to prevent leftovers from becoming notar — proof the Sages DO care about wasting consecrated items
This baraita reflects only the RABBIS' view, not Rebbi's — so it doesn't disprove Rebbi's position
If Rebbi truly holds 'no ordinance for consecrated items,' does this baraita refute him?
No — Rebbi can still hold his view for the specific sin-offering scenario; the meal-offering rule is a separate halakha

callout.label: Key move:
callout.text: A general concern for preventing waste (as in the meal-offering case) doesn't automatically mean every sage endorses a specific 'ordinance' resolving THIS dispute the same way.

slides.title: 🐐 The Yom Kippur Goats Test Rabbi Abba's Framing
slides.subtitle: A second pair's sin-offering goat, treated like an animal 'designated to replace a loss'

lines.speaker: Mishna (Yoma)
lines.text: If the scapegoat dies, a new pair is drawn. The High Priest atones with the SECOND pair's sin-offering goat; the first pair's surviving goat grazes until blemished — since it's a COMMUNAL offering, it doesn't die.

lines.speaker: Inference
lines.text: This implies: were it an INDIVIDUAL's offering, it WOULD die. But the second-pair goat is like a replacement for something 'lost' (the first goat, functionally rejected) — and atonement is being achieved through the REPLACEMENT, not the lost one!

lines.speaker: Problem for Rabbi Abba
lines.text: Rabbi Abba says everyone agrees: atonement via the NON-lost (i.e., the replacement) means the lost one simply dies — no dispute needed here at all. So why would this scenario even reflect Rebbi's view specifically?

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: This mishna must follow Rebbi ALONE — since only Rebbi holds that 'designating a replacement for something functionally lost' counts as if the ORIGINAL were lost, making the first-pair goat's death-by-default meaningful only under his view.

callout.label: The deeper point:
callout.text: Rav's own principle — 'living animals are not [permanently] rejected' — determines which goat ultimately provides atonement, feeding directly into this dispute.

slides.title: 🔄 The Mishna Itself Seems to Refute BOTH Views
slides.subtitle: Resolved by one elegant principle about what a mishna chooses to teach

steps.content: 1️⃣ The mishna says: lost animal, replacement SACRIFICED, original found → dies. It says nothing about consulting the court, or about which one achieved atonement
2️⃣ By implication: if the replacement was NOT yet sacrificed, the original simply grazes — regardless of who consulted whom, regardless of which animal is 'the lost one'
3️⃣ This seems to refute BOTH Rav Huna (who needs 'consulting the court' to matter) AND Rabbi Abba (who needs 'atoning via the lost one' to matter)!

4️⃣ Resolution: the mishna teaches only the ABSOLUTE, unconditional case (sacrifice always causes death) — and simply omits the more nuanced, disputed scenarios that depend on those specific variables

callout.label: A second identical challenge:
callout.text: The exact same pattern of refutation-and-resolution recurs for the mishna's parallel case about lost MONEY (rather than an animal) — settled the same way.

slides.title: 💰 Money Set Aside 'As a Guarantee' — Not to Replace a Loss
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Ami's ruling, and why it specifically matters for Rabbi Shimon

boxes.title: For Rebbi and the Rabbis
items: Both agree: money designated as a mere GUARANTEE (not to replace something already lost) funds communal gifts if unused
For Rebbi: obvious, since his stringent 'dies/Dead Sea' rule applies only to true replacement-for-loss cases
For the Rabbis: an a fortiori inference — if even replacement-for-loss money isn't treated as 'lost,' surely guarantee-money isn't either

boxes.title: For Rabbi Shimon
items: Rabbi Shimon is MORE stringent — ANY atonement via a second animal kills the first, no exceptions
One might think he'd extend this even to mere 'guarantee' money

Rabbi Ami teaches: even Rabbi Shimon concedes guarantee-money funds communal gifts — proven from the Temple's own thirteen collection horns, six of which funded such gift offerings (per Rabbi Yehuda's report, defended against Rabbi Neḥemya's challenge via Yehoyada the priest's own teaching)

callout.label: Why Rabbi Ami's ruling was needed:
callout.text: Without it, one might assume Rabbi Shimon's stringency about REPLACEMENT-for-loss money extends to simple GUARANTEE money too — he teaches that even Rabbi Shimon draws this line.

summary.principle: The Rebbi/Rabbis dispute over a lost-then-replaced sin offering can be framed either around consulting the court (Rav Huna) or around which animal achieves atonement (Rabbi Abba), and the mishna's own wording — teaching only the clear-cut case — leaves room for both framings, while money set aside merely as insurance is treated more leniently than money replacing a genuine loss even by the strictest opinion.

flowSteps.content: ⚖️ Two framings of the dispute: consulting the court (Rav Huna) vs. which animal atones (Rabbi Abba)
🍞🐐 Each framing tested against outside sources, surviving only by careful attribution to one sage

columns.content: 🔄 Mishna's own wording teaches only the absolute case, leaving both framings possible
💰 Guarantee money vs. replacement-for-loss money — even Rabbi Shimon distinguishes them

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: a mishna's silence on a variable doesn't refute a position — it may simply be teaching only the clear-cut case

quiz.q: According to Rav Huna's framing, what determines the Rebbi/Rabbis dispute?
o: Which animal was born first
Whether the owner consulted the court before sacrificing one of the two available animals, versus just taking one and sacrificing it without asking
The color of the animals
Whether the animals are male or female
quiz.e: Rav Huna holds that everyone agrees an animal taken and sacrificed without consulting the court causes the other to die; the dispute is only about what the court should advise when consulted.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Abba's framing, what determines the Rebbi/Rabbis dispute?
o: Whether the animal was female
Whether atonement was achieved specifically through the LOST animal (Rebbi says the replacement then also dies) or through the non-lost one (agreed by all: the lost one dies)
The value of the animals
Whether the owner was a priest
quiz.e: Rabbi Abba holds everyone agrees atonement via the non-lost animal causes the lost one to die; the dispute is only about achieving atonement via the ORIGINALLY lost animal, and whether the replacement is then treated as 'the lost one' too.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara resolve the challenge that the mishna's own wording seems to refute BOTH Rav Huna's and Rabbi Abba's framings?
o: It concludes both framings are wrong and rejects them entirely
It explains the mishna teaches only the absolute, unconditional case (sacrifice causes death) and simply omits the more nuanced disputed scenarios
It says the mishna text is corrupted
It says only Rav Huna survives the challenge
quiz.e: The Gemara's resolution is that a mishna need not spell out every disputed nuance — here it teaches only the clear-cut case where the replacement WAS sacrificed, leaving the more contested scenarios for other sources to address.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Ami, what happens to unused money that was designated merely 'as a guarantee' (not to replace something already lost)?
o: It must be cast into the Dead Sea
It is allocated for communal gift offerings — even according to Rabbi Shimon's generally stricter view
It can never be used for any purpose
It automatically becomes the property of the priests
quiz.e: Rabbi Ami teaches that even Rabbi Shimon, who is generally stringent about atonement disqualifying the other resource, concedes that mere guarantee-money (not replacing a genuine loss) funds communal gift offerings when unused.

quiz.q: What Temple detail does the Gemara cite to prove that Rabbi Shimon does hold surplus sin/guilt-offering funds can become communal gift offerings (נְדָבָה)?
o: The design of the Temple menorah
The thirteen collection horns in the Temple, six of which were designated for communal gift offerings — supported by Yehoyada the priest's teaching on 'it is a guilt offering'
The layout of the Holy of Holies
The schedule of priestly watches
quiz.e: The Gemara cites the mishna about the Temple's thirteen shofar-shaped collection horns, six of which funded communal gift offerings from surplus sin/guilt-offering money, defended by Yehoyada's own teaching that such surplus should fund burnt offerings.
